item.title: US and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump's 'annihilation' threat
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck62m1631d7po?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US and Iran hold first talks since June after Trump's 'annihilation' threat - Published Top Iranian and US officials have held talks at the UN in New York on a day when the US leader said he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if the conflict went unresolved. No breakthrough has been reported from the meeting mediated by Qatar and involving Iran's foreign minister and US President Donald Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff - the first since a June ceasefire unravelled. Witkoff said a round of discussions had been completed "that we hope will prove constructive and promising". Iran repeated its demand for the US to end its "acts of aggression". The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz. Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of prices. It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November. In his address at the annual meeting of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, Trump began by touting his accomplishments on the economy, immigration, the border and tackling violent crime - remarks that sounded more pitched to voters the US midterms than the diplomats in the hall. He spent much of his address justifying the war with Iran - a huge contrast with remarks earlier by UN Secretary General António Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening and underscored the "interdependence" of the world's peoples. The US president argued that the conflict had prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and demonstrated the value of what he described as peace through strength - ultimatums rather than deal-making or compromise. "Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said. "Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?" Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections. The remarks were indicative of his foreign-policy strategy of coercive diplomacy - threatening overwhelming force while keeping negotiations open. Trump later told reporters that American officials had had a "very productive" three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the general assembly. Iran state TV confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had met Witkoff. Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, quoted by state broadcaster IRNA, later said negotiations took part through a Qatari mediator who communicated Tehran's conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts and to US "acts of aggression". The BBC asked Witkoff how the meetings had gone as he was leaving the UN building and he responded with a thumbs up. Witkoff later confirmed on X that the talks had been held "through the mediators, who shuttled between the two sides throughout the day". "They successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising," Witkoff said. "The mediators will continue their work." Since the ceasefire collapsed, both sides have intermittently exchanged fire. Iran has attacked vessels it says have attempted to cross the Strait of Hormuz without authorisation. The US has attacked Iranian sites in the strait - as well as Iranian tankers off the country's coast. The US has also maintained a blockade of Iranian ports, causing a huge disruption to the Iranian economy. In an effort to force Tehran to agree a deal to end the conflict, President Trump has also threatened sanctions against any country that continues trading with Iran. But so far, there has been no indication of a change of course in Iran, which insists the US and Israel end their war, including against the Iran-backed Shia group Hezbollah in Lebanon which Israel has been attacking. Yemen's Houthis - also allied to Iran - have recently intesified attacks aimed at disrupting oil shipping from Saudi Arabia, promting an escalation of the conflict with the kingdom. - Published5 days ago

item.title: Reports of violence against women in Gaza surge, UN agency finds
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c94gm7dp40y0o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Reports of violence against women in Gaza surge, UN agency finds - Published There has been a sharp rise in reports of violence against women and girls in the Gaza Strip, including early and forced marriage, according to a series of recent reports from the UN Population Fund (UNFPA). One report, which analyses data collected by 10 organisations, says, external the protracted crisis in war-torn Gaza has "created conditions in which women and girls face escalating risks of gender-based violence". It also warns that there has been a "severe escalation" in the number of early and forced marriage incidents in the second quarter of this year. Both are considered types of gender-based violence (GBV) by the UN. Another report presenting testimony from 230 women in crowded displacement camps in Gaza City and Khan Younis, external makes for a grim read, describing the violence they have experienced or witnessed. Some readers may find some of the details in this report distressing One displaced woman in a school-turned-shelter in Gaza highlights how rape victims are often married to their rapists to avoid shame and scandal. "When rape cases are discovered in schools, you find weddings and celebrations at the school the next day," she says. Another woman tells how last year, at the time of famine, "a man married off his 14-year-old daughter in exchange for two bags of flour so he and his [other] children could eat". Six women in different displacement camps shared stories of such exchanges - which would have been unthinkable before the conflict between Israel and Hamas began in 2023. Although data collection to establish actual figures remains tricky, in the second quarter of this year, the UNFPA says the number of reported cases of early and forced marriage had increased by 123% on the first quarter. Early or child marriage involved girls aged 12 to 17. "The trends are shocking," says Nestor Owomuhangi, the UNFPA representative to Palestine. He says that the extreme circumstances over the past three years - which have seen tens of thousands of people killed, mass destruction and multiple waves of displacement in Gaza - have broken down social structures, so "everything is eroded... there is no system". While food markets have reopened, many cannot afford the goods on offer, there is still extreme poverty and hunger with reliance on charitable handouts. Nearly all the population of more than two million Gazans have been driven from their homes, leaving most living in squalid tent camps or damaged buildings. Public services have largely collapsed, and Israeli air strikes have continued despite the ceasefire. Prior to the war, girls in Gaza outnumbered and outperformed boys at every level of education above primary school. Now, with prolonged school closures, many children have dropped out of education. For boys there is pressure to find informal work to help support their families, for girls there are heightened issues around safety. Living among strangers, without privacy, in a socially conservative society, there are complaints of heightened sexual harassment and abuse - many families see marrying their daughters as a way to protect them and preserve modesty. The UNFPA report - based on research carried out in late 2025 and early 2026 - reveals how girls orphaned during the war are especially vulnerable. One woman in a Gaza City camp interviewed for the report says she attended the wedding of two girls from her family, aged just 14 and 15. "Their uncles married them off very young. Do you know why? Because their father and mother were martyred, and their uncles wanted to get rid of the responsibility and expenses," the woman said. "By God, they don't understand what marriage or life is." The Women's Affairs Center in Gaza - a Palestinian NGO which works with the UNFPA - and other support groups have documented distressing cases of girls who have been married and suffered abuse, often becoming pregnant. They say that those in their early teens are much more likely to have miscarriages and underweight babies than adult women. "We see adolescent pregnancies going through the roof because of child marriage," says Owomuhangi. "A child who is at an age when the body is not fully developed to sustain another body, who is hungry, in unhygienic circumstances, who doesn't know how to take care of the infant, who doesn't even know how to take care of herself, the consequences of that pregnancy are always really, really bad." The UN and most humanitarian organisations categorise marriages of girls under 18 as early marriage. Even before the war, this was more common among Palestinians in Hamas-run Gaza than it was in the occupied West Bank, but it was declining. The law in Gaza allows exceptions to the minimum marital age of 17 with parental consent and authorisation by a judge. Court officials can approve marriage for those as young as 14 years and seven months old, although a local Sharia expert told us that "legal safeguards" had been removed when Islamic courts - which officiate over family matters for Muslims - were closed for a large part of the war. The BBC has been speaking to some families in which bereaved relatives were married. Zuhair, who is 25, says his uncles pushed him to marry a 16-year-old girl from his extended family after her father - her sole guardian - was killed in an Israeli air strike. Challenged on why he agreed to go ahead with the plan, he said: "One of the reasons that led me to marry her was that there was no one to take care of her. That's the first point." "If it were not for the war, she would still be a young girl spoiled by her father. She would be going to school," Zuhair adds. "She still has a child's mindset, not a mature mindset. She misses school, her family, friends. She even misses simply sitting at home." A couple says they allowed their 17-year-old son to marry his 16-year-old cousin after their older son and the girl's father were killed. The teenager is now pregnant so will not return to school. "She needs to care for her child," her father-in-law says, "her education would be in vain." Sexual violence in Gaza remains acutely under-reported in large part due to fear of stigma and retaliation. UN safety audits have shown particular risks to women and girls at night, causing them to avoid camp toilets and bathrooms. The latest analysis report by the UNFPA-led task force stated that incidents of sexual violence, including rape and sexual assault, "have become critical in Gaza". They accounted for 2.7% of total reported incidents of GBV from April to June 2026 - up from 2.1% in the quarter before; this represented a 61% surge in absolute case numbers. This rise is being linked to efforts to raise awareness and provide better ways to make confidential reports. Demographic data indicated that the majority of survivors were women aged 18-59, followed by adolescent girls at 8% and adult men at 5%. Women who are widows or have husbands who are detained or missing are at increased risk of sexual abuse and exploitation. Nearly one in four households is now reportedly headed by a woman - double the proportion before the war. "One widow was looking for a tent, and a [camp] representative told her, "I'll give you a tent, we'll put you in our camp, and you can come stay with me tonight," recalls a woman in Gaza City, interviewed for the UNFPA report. Aid agencies argue that the dangers for women in Gaza could be greatly eased by improving humanitarian conditions. There are calls for Israel to allow higher quality shelters into the territory as well as equipment to upgrade latrines and sanitation as well as lighting. Israel restricts items it classes as having a potential dual use for military purposes. There are ongoing efforts to improve education and healthcare and longer-term plans for campaigns to combat domestic violence and child marriage. While the course of so many lives in Gaza has already been permanently changed, women say they hope for a future in which they at least feel safer. If you have been affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available in the UK at BBC Action Line.

item.title: Ethiopia and Tigray accuse each of launching offensives, fuelling fears of new war
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cry8zwwq21pxo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Ethiopia and Tigray accuse each of launching offensives, fuelling fears of new war - Published Ethiopia's government and the party in control of the northern region of Tigray have accused each other of launching offensives, escalating fears of a return to full-scale conflict. Getachew Reda, a cabinet minister and adviser to Ethiopia's prime minister, said Tigrayan fighters had taken control of federally administered airports in Tigray and launched offensives in neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. Earlier, the Tigrayan authorities said their forces had been forced to enter a "defensive war". The statement followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray. The two-year war in Tigray ended in 2022 - but over recent months both sides have been accusing each other of violating a peace deal. It was one of the most deadly conflicts this century - the African Union's mediator estimated some 600,000 people died as the fighting drove the region to the precipice of famine. On Sunday, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray, announced an alliance with six other armed groups in Ethiopia to remove the government in Addis Ababa. - Seven Ethiopian rebel groups form new alliance - Published1 day ago "It is rather heartbreaking to learn that, despite efforts by many, including the international community, to avoid yet another round of war in Tigray, the TPLF leadership early this morning launched an all-out offensive against government positions in Afar and Amhara," Getachew said in a statement shared on social media. The adviser to Prime Minster Abiy Ahmed previously led Tigray's interim administration, but he fell out with the TPLF in 2025 and joined the federal government. Following the seizure of the airports, Ethiopian Airlines has cancelled all flights to Tigray. Residents of Tigray's main city of Mekelle told the BBC that local forces had taken over control of the city's airport from the national police early on Wednesday. This followed reports of drone strikes in Tigray in recent days. On Tuesday, a strike in the southern town of Alamata killed at least 14 people and injured 22 others, according to the Tigrayan authorities. The town's mayor, Mogos Shiferaw, told the BBC that more than five drones and one fighter jet had carried out more than 21 strikes starting at around 03:30. "This caused a lot of psychological trauma in our city and our people were in a state of panic," he said. Mogos said all those killed and injured were civilians, accusing federal forces of targeting two secondary schools. He believed they were struck on suspicion that they were being used by Tigrayan forces. But the mayor said the schools, which had served as federal military bases during the civil war, were unoccupied as the academic year had not yet begun. The BBC has not independently verified the allegations and the government has not commented on the alleged strikes. On Wednesday, the Tigray authorities accused Addis Ababa of launching an "open invasion" of the region, urging people to support the regional forces and maintain unity. It further accused the government of violating international humanitarian and human rights laws, saying public services and critical infrastructure had been disrupted. Meanwhile, the US State Department's Bureau of African Affairs has condemned a separate drone strike that it said took place on Monday, targeting a convoy of Catholic vehicles carrying food aid. It called for an investigation and urged all parties to resolve their differences through dialogue and take steps to prevent similar incidents. Both Addis Ababa and TPLF leaders have faced criticism over delays in implementing key provisions of the Pretoria Agreement, the AU-brokered deal that formally ended the conflict in November 2022. In July, Prime Minister Abiy accused the TPLF of preparing for renewed conflict during an address to parliament. Just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, the TPLF restored its pre-war administration, disbanding an interim one appointed by Abiy. There have also been reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its forces. item.title: Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vgy55lm8z1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage - Published The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman from the home in Madrid where she lived for seven decades has drawn attention to the depth of Spain's housing crisis. The tenant of the flat in the Retiro area of central Madrid, Maricarmen, was unable to pay the rent set by the investment firm that owns it. Maricarmen's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a cap on the rent. However, the company that bought the property in 2018, Urbagestión, cited a legal glitch allowing it to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650. It subsequently lowered the new rent to €1,650 but Maricarmen was still unable to pay it with her monthly pension of €1,350. Three previous attempts to evict her were blocked by the courts and the case has received increasing media attention. Supporters of Maricarmen camped outside the building on Tuesday night, joined by celebrities including Javier Bardem's brother, Carlos, and the singer Ana Belén, who read out the poem Desahucio (Eviction) by Rafael Alberti. Several hundred people, mostly youngsters, had gathered by the morning in a bid to prevent the eviction from taking place, chanting "Maricarmen stays". Some activists blocked the stairs inside the building. In a video posted on social media, a tearful Maricarmen thanked those who had come out to support her against "this cruel struggle by someone who wants to earn money". - The hard men removing squatters in Spain - Published26 August 2021 - Taking back Barcelona's apartments - Published12 December 2015 - 'Sometimes I want to cry': Eviction in a pandemic - Published14 December 2020 Police cordoned off a section of the street and removed people from the entrance to the building, including members of the media, striking some protesters with batons. A representative of tenants' organisation Sindicato de Inquilinas shouted at the police through a megaphone: "Think for 10 seconds about Maricarmen, who could be your own grandmother." "There is a police deployment as if this were a military operation," said Beatriz Duro, Maricarmen's lawyer. "This is the fourth time [they've tried to evict her] but the first time they've come right to the door of the property. It's completely disproportionate." In June, the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights called for the pensioner's eviction to be halted and for her to be offered affordable alternative accommodation. The local government said she had declined its offer of a place in an elderly care home. The central government said Urbagestión had refused its repeated attempts to negotiate Maricarmen's situation. The BBC has attempted to contact the company. The possibility of a last-minute reprieve for Maricarmen appeared when an anonymous donor offered to pay most of her rent. However, Urbagestión reportedly rejected the offer and the eviction went ahead. "Today is a very sad day, a very dramatic day, when it's plain to see the effects of unbridled speculation, of not wanting to control the market, of putting out the red carpet for the vultures and the speculators," said Housing Minister Teresa Rodríguez. A shortage of available housing has been blamed for soaring rental costs in recent years, which have left millions of Spaniards struggling to find affordable homes. In Madrid, rentals have increased by more than 100% over the last decade, according to property site Idealista, with a 10% rise over the last year. The Socialist-led government of Pedro Sánchez has frequently targeted companies whose investment pushes up housing costs. In January, the prime minister said he aimed to "protect those who are most exposed to that speculation and that greed". However, some critics of the government say it needs to work harder to build new homes, and others warn that its rhetoric discourages many owners from placing their properties on the rental market.

item.title: Dolly Parton's manager accuses her nephew of 'threats and intimidation'
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c670lydl5wg5o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Dolly Parton's manager accuses her nephew of 'threats and intimidation' - Published Dolly Parton's management company has accused her nephew of "threats, intimidation, and coercion", revealing a bitter battle over the late star's legacy and business interests. The accusations against Bryan Seaver, who was Parton's head of security and was handpicked to announce her death last month, have been made public in US legal documents filed this week. The company that manages Parton's businesses and properties, She's Alive, is seeking a temporary civil restraining order against him. In court filings, She's Alive alleged that Seaver mounted "an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats", claiming he said he would ruin her empire if the estate did not pay him. He has denied the claims. In a statement to TMZ, external, he said that text messages and emails quoted in the court application had been taken out of context to make it look like he was threatening people. "Nothing in this lawsuit were threats and most of the comments I stand by," he said. "A lot of these messages are two guys having rage talk and crying on the phone together while we were grieving." Seaver, the son of Parton's sister Cassie, owns a company that provided the singer's security detail for the last 20 years of her life. Last week, he was fired by She's Alive as head of security for her properties. In a statement at the time, Seaver and his company said the dismissal was "unexpected" and "unexplained". They added: "We refuse to be intimidated by those whose actions we believe are being taken in bad faith and with the intent to profit from the life of someone who willingly gave so much." The request for a restraining order was filed in Nashville on Tuesday by She's Alive, which is run by Parton's longtime manager Danny Nozell. The court documents quoted a series of exchanges in which someone, identified by the estate as Seaver, threatened to destroy Parton's brand. In one, he's alleged to have said he would become "the hand of retribution for my entire family", according to the court documents. Another said: "I'm going to set up a podcast dedicated to ruining Dolly's brand partnerships and telling the violations these people have done on us. It's going to be great. Or [expletive] pay me." The papers also claimed that Seaver used his experience as a military contractor to intimidate employees. In an exchange with one of Parton's lawyers, he allegedly described himself as a "killer" and said that on the day his aunt died, he had sold $27m (£20m) in arms and ammunition to the Haitian police. "All I do is warfare... Everyone needs to be worried about what I might do," he was accused of saying, according to a copy of an email attached to the complaint. In his statement published on TMZ, Seaver said: "I am a career soldier and military contractor and do conduct arms deals for foreign governments. I am a security professional and I am a killer." But he denied making threats and said he had been "talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend". The messages have resulted in some employees and lawyers for Parton's trusts and estates resigning, according to the court documents. She's Alive has also had to hire private security for its employees, including at their homes, the filing states. The BBC has contacted Seaver and She's Alive for further comment. Parton's roadmap Previously, Seaver was known to the public for announcing his aunt's death in a video posted to her Instagram account on 25 August. Speaking in front of a black background, he was sombre and reflective as he introduced himself and shared the unexpected news. "This video announcement is something Dolly asked of me years ago, before I fully absorbed it as a future reality," he said in the video. Seaver added that he had followed in his father Larry's footsteps in becoming Parton's head of security, a post he held for more than 20 years. Nozell started working for Parton in 2004, first as a tour consultant and later as her manager. In the 2019 Netflix film, Dolly Parton: Here I Am, he said his job was to transform her from a "heritage act" into a "superstar", and he took responsibility for reviving her international touring career. In a statement last month, he said the singer had "worked up until the day she died" on multiple projects, and envisioned a legacy that continued long beyond her death. "She loved seeing her dreams come to life, and loved knowing her work brought people joy," he said in the statement. "Ever the planner, Dolly worked with the team that she handpicked, for the past several years to build a project roadmap that will guide us for decades to come." The estate now faces a public tug of war over that legacy. Related topics - Published31 August - Published26 August

item.title: Poland accuses Russian military helicopter of violating its airspace
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c699d2dn9z0mo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Poland accuses Russian military helicopter of violating its airspace - Published Poland has said a Russian military helicopter briefly violated its airspace, forcing the Nato member to scramble fighter jets while ground forces remained on alert. Its military said the Mi-8 aircraft had crossed from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on Wednesday morning, penetrating Polish airspace to a depth of about 300 metres (328 yards) and staying for 42 seconds north of Braniewo. It said "the nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defence". Moscow did not comment immediately. Poland and other European Nato members have recently said Russia may be preparing attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine - Moscow denies this. Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Moscow does not plan to attack Nato states. By contrast, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said this month that it was Europe that was constantly talking about preparing for war, and he warned: "If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war [from that in Ukraine], and it will be very short." Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory, including the Crimea peninsula annexed in 2014. In a statement, the Polish Army Operational Command said the brief incursion had happened at 11:08 (09:08 GMT), and the helicopter had been tracked by radar. Poland's air defence units were operating around the clock ready to "ensure the safety of Polish airspace", it added. A number of Russian drones and one unarmed Russian missile have landed in Poland since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which is not a member of Nato. Last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggested Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank. "In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans... has intensified," he said. "The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine." French President Emmanuel Macron said shortly afterwards that his country had been targeted by Russian hybrid attacks in the past few weeks, vowing that this would not be left "without a response". Macron said he had already ordered a plan to protect the country's critical infrastructure and defence industry sites. Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary. These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary. There have recently been a number of suspicious fires and blasts at defence facilities in a number of European Nato members from Italy to Bulgaria to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia. Earlier this month, Germany said Russia was responsible for August's drone attack at Leipzig airport - an accusation denied by Moscow as "absurd". And earlier this week, Lithuania's prime minister told the BBC that his country had already made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they would "not surrender" if attacked. Ukraine said the drone's target "could have been the diplomatic train", while the Russian military said only that it had struck "railway infrastructure". - Published7 August - Published6 February 2023

item.title: Eleven killed in mass shooting at house in South Africa
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crgjqxzl097eo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Eleven killed in mass shooting at house in South Africa - Published At least 11 people have been killed in a mass shooting in a residential building near the South African city of Durban. Gunmen stormed a house in the KwaMakhutha township late on Tuesday and opened fire on 14 people. Ten were killed at the scene and four were taken to hospital, where one later died from their injuries, police said. Police said some of the victims were on their watch in connection with illegal activities, which they could not "divulge at the moment to protect investigations which have been launched". While the motive of the shooting has not yet been confirmed, the police said they could not rule out a "feud between rival groupings". "Information available at this stage suggests that 13 men and one woman, who is believed to be pregnant, were reportedly having a party inside a house when three men arrived and opened fire on them," the police said in a statement. The woman is among those who died. A local TV reporter from the eNCA channel at the scene said the gunmen had set fire to a vehicle belonging to one of the victims before fleeing, with footage showing the burnt-out car. The police say they have launched a manhunt for the suspects, who were said to be carrying pistols and rifles. South Africa has one of the world's highest murder rates, with police data showing a murder rate equivalent to more than 60 deaths a day. In recent weeks, the gruesome discovery of at least nine murdered women, with some of the bodies dumped by the roadside, has heightened fears in the country. Last year, nine people were killed in a mass shooting at a tavern in Johannesburg. Rivalry among criminal gangs amid turf wars, drug trafficking and illegal mining is common in the country, often driving violence within communities. In February, President Cyril Ramaphosa said organised crime was "the most immediate threat to our democracy, our society and our economic development", as he announced that he would be deploying the army to support the police. Although South Africa has long had a high murder rate, mass shootings are a more recent problem and elicit increased feelings of unsafety, fear and shock. The phenomenon has led to calls for the government and law enforcement authorities to do more to dismantle organised crime networks and, in some cases, "murder for hire" syndicates – believed to be among the leading instigators of the attacks. Much has also been said about improving the economic conditions that make crime an attractive enterprise for some. There are no easy answers for how to solve South Africa's crime problem but security experts believe that the high proliferation of illegal guns, insufficient visible policing in high crime spots, the slow pace of justice and allegations that senior politicians and police officers have links to criminal gangs all add to the pervasive sentiment that local authorities are losing the fight against crime. item.title: Trump administration accuses banned media outlets of 'falsehoods' ahead of court hearing
item.description:

Trump administration accuses banned media outlets of 'falsehoods' ahead of court hearing - Published The US Justice Department has filed documents that accuse three media outlets banned from the White House of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods" and reporting which "threatened national security" as it prepared to defend the move in court. Last week, President Donald Trump barred CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news". After their reporters had their passes confiscated and were denied access to the building, the three outlets jointly launched legal action, calling the move unconstitutional. On Wednesday, a judge is set to decide whether to issue an order temporarily lifting the ban, pending a full hearing. According to a court filing by the Justice Department in a District of Columbia court, the three outlets were issued with a list of "reporting incidents" by the White House ahead of the ban. The filing cites a number of stories about construction at the White House - including about a security bunker and the building of a new ballroom, as well as a report on an internal information leak investigation. It goes on to say that "access to the White House is a privilege, not a right". The three media organisations have argued that the ban breaches their rights under the First Amendment, which forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press. In a joint statement confirming legal action against the government, they said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. "Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference." Major TV networks have withdrawn from a media-sharing arrangement of video and images of the president, known as the pool, in protest over the ban. Shortly after, the White House launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, which operates a 24/7 feed of clips of the president. On Tuesday, tensions continued between Trump and some of the news outlets, as Trump told CNN reporter Kaitlin Collins before his speech to the United Nations General Assembly: "I'm surprised that CNN is here covering me. You should not be here covering me. You said you weren't going to cover me." Collins noted later on air that the network had made no such pledge. He also took to social media to attack Collins, once again asking why she and others were reporting on the president at the UN. The US president also hit out again at CNN , Politico and MS NOW, calling them "treasonous". Related topics - Published20 hours ago - Published3 days ago

item.title: Azerbaijan pardons Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire

========================================
Azerbaijan pardons Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire - Published French national Martin Ryan has been pardoned and his release from prison ordered by Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev after he was jailed on charges of spying. His release came hours after the EU agreed to lift sanctions on two Russian billionaires, prompting anger from Ukraine. Diplomats had indicated that France had pushed for an end to restrictions on one of the businessmen, Alisher Usmanov. Ryan, who denied espionage, is one of 20 people pardoned by Aliyev. However, a second Frenchman, Anass Derraz, remains in jail in Azerbaijan accused of accepting a Russian bribe. It was not clear what had led to pressure for sanctions on Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov to be lifted - the EU also agreed to take Russian-Israeli oligarch Mikhail Fridman off its sanctions list. Slovakia is understood to have pressed for Usmanov's name to removed initially, and France then backed the move, highlighting national security concerns. Both men have been under EU embargo since the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and until now EU sanctions on more than 3,000 "individuals and entities" have had to be renewed every six months. The latest agreement extends the sanctions on the others for three years. Usmanov was cited by the EU in its 2022 listing, external as having "particularly close ties" to Russia's President Vladimir Putin, and of having "supported materially or financially and benefited from Russian decision-makers responsible for the annexation of Crimea and the destabilisation of Ukraine". The metals and mining billionaire denied this characterisation of him. He has also been sanctioned by the UK and US governments. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha bitterly criticised the EU decision to lift sanctions on the two men, complaining that Moscow was "celebrating, because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans". Latvia had initially opposed the move, but decided to abstain, announcing instead that it would impose its own measures on the two men. Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said it was "dangerous and sends completely the wrong signal at a time when Russia's behaviour is becoming more aggressive". Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said later that France's President Emmanuel Macron had agreed to start talks on Latvia's "accession to the French nuclear deterrence initiative". French relations with Azerbaijan have been poor in recent years, largely because of France's close relations with neighbouring Armenia. However, in May, Macron discussed developing ties with Aliyev, who later spoke of a "new era" in their relations. Under Aliyev's decree on Wednesday, Ryan is one of 20 people including Azerbaijanis and Turks given a pardon. Detained in December 2023, he was handed a 10-year jail term last March for espionage, charges denied by the French government. Prosecutors alleged he had co-operated with employees of France's security services in Baku and gathered information about Azerbaijan's relations with Turkey, Iran and Pakistan, as well as companies linked to Russia and China. "I did not spy. I am not a spy, and during the court case I tried to prove this," Ryan had told the court. Another man he went on trial with, Azad Mamedli, was given 12 years in jail. Mamedli was not among the 20 prisoners pardoned by Aliyev. - Published20 hours ago - Published16 March

Trump meets US-backed Venezuelan president for first time since Maduro seized - Published US President Donald Trump has held talks with Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodríguez at the UN General Assembly, their first face-to-face meeting since the White House backed her to take over the South American country's government. Rodríguez succeeded Nicolás Maduro shortly after US forces conducted a raid on the Venezuelan capital Caracas and seized him. The pair met a few kilometres from the New York jail where Maduro is awaiting trial for drug trafficking and other charges. Rodríguez said they discussed "advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, and security". US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles also attended the meeting. Rodríguez's government has signed an agreement allowing the US to control more than 65 billion barrels of its oil - more than a fifth of the country's reserves. It grants a US-led company 100-year concessions over 17 oilfields in Venezuela. Trump previously called it "the biggest oil deal in world history". During his address to the UN on Monday, Trump said the US and Venezuela control "more than 60%" of the world's oil, adding: "To the victor belong the spoils." Rodríguez is due to address the UN on Wednesday. She previously served as vice-president to Maduro and was sanctioned by the US in 2018, but the measures were lifted in April this year. She was sworn in as interim president by Venezuela's National Assembly days after the US raid with the White House's blessing. item.title: South Sudan's president dissolves government ahead of country's first elections
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8750ykkglq1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
South Sudan's president dissolves government ahead of country's first elections - Published South Sudan President Salva Kiir has dissolved the transitional government, three months before the country's first election since its independence in 2011. The country has previously postponed elections twice and extended the transitional period several times. Under the amended law, signed on Monday, Kiir removed the country's five vice-presidents and dissolved parliament, as well as national and state governments. Kiir is the presidential candidate of his Sudan People's Liberation Movement (SPLM). No prominent figures have announced plans to challenge him in the December poll. The main opposition leader Riek Machar was sacked as vice-president last year and charged with treason. He is under house arrest. Machar had been named vice-president as part of a 2018 peace deal to end a five-year civil war between forces loyal to the two men. Kiir will remain in office with full constitutional powers until an elected president is sworn in. He also reappointed some ministers and governors in caretaker positions until the 22 December elections. Ahead of Tuesday's announcement a heavy security presence was reported in the capital, Juba. Soldiers from the army and national security services blocked access to government ministries. Soldiers were also seen patrolling parts of the city. A senior government official told the BBC that staff arriving for work were turned away and told to return the following Monday. UN agencies in Juba also asked staff to work remotely while the situation was monitored. - South Sudan's leader sacks aides after dead man appointed - Published3 February Kiir last week dismissed the chairman of the national elections commission, Abednego Akok Kacuol, without giving a reason. He was replaced by the commission's secretary-general, Gabriel Bol Deng. Akok had said in August that the commission needed $250m (£190m) to conduct the election but had received only $21m. In June, the main opposition group, the Sudan People's Liberation Movement in Opposition (SPLM-IO), the party of Machar, warned people not to take part in poll preparations. "Anyone coming to register voters and campaign in territories controlled by the mighty SPLM-IO, you will be a prisoner of war," Nathaniel Pierino, acting chairperson of the group, said in a post on Facebook. The body which oversees implementation of the 2018 peace agreement, the Reconstituted Joint Monitoring and Evaluation Commission (RJMEC), said South Sudan had entered a "critical phase". It said several key talks under the agreement remained incomplete and urged the parties to agree on a path towards credible elections and a peaceful end to the transitional period, which has lasted since independence. The latest 24-month extension was due to end on 22 February 2027. item.title: Hurricane Polo downgraded but remains 'very powerful' off coast of Mexico
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckddvlrlr5qeo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Hurricane Polo downgraded but remains 'very powerful' off coast of Mexico - Published Hurricane Polo, a large storm off the coast of Mexico, has been downgraded to category 4 but remains "very powerful", the US National Hurricane Center said. The Pacific hurricane, one of the strongest of the season, was projected to head towards the coast of south-western Mexico, bringing intense wind and rain, though was not expected to make landfall. A Hurricane Hunter aircraft, operated by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa), flew into the storm on Tuesday and recorded sustained wind speeds near 180 mph (285 km/h), with stronger gusts. The slow-moving storm is being fuelled by extremely warm waters caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon. It was previously a category 5 storm - the highest level on the scale - but was downgraded to category 4 on Wednesday morning. As it slowly drifts north west, Polo will drive torrential rainfall in parts of Mexico's south-west coast, and "may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the forecaster said. Rainfall totals of up to 6in (15cm) are forecast, with 8in possible in some areas. Residents have also been warned of large ocean swells and life-threatening surf conditions for the next few days. "So far, the information we have is that (Polo) will not make a direct landfall on the coast," Mexico's President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Tuesday, but she warned residents along the Pacific coast to be vigilant. Sheinbaum highlighted the states of Jalisco, Colima and Michoacan as being at risk. Data from the Hurricane Hunter aircraft indicated that Polo could still strengthen, because of what NOAA called a "very conducive" environment of extremely warm ocean waters feeding the storm. Scientists monitoring the ocean temperatures say the current El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record. Daily sea surface temperatures in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific were 3.05C above average on 19 September - exceeding the previous record of 3.02C set during the very strong El Niño of 2015. Some longer-term measures of El Niño have not yet hit record levels but this is likely to change, with the peak not expected until later this year. Warmer ocean waters mean storms can pick up more energy, leading to higher wind speeds. El Niño is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year. Trade winds that typically blow from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards. Heat is then released from the ocean into the atmosphere which can boost global temperatures and drive changes in weather patterns around the world. Related topics - Published1 day ago

item.title: OpenAI gives cyber defence tools to Ukraine
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c90kly26d7pzo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
OpenAI gives cyber defence tools to Ukraine - Published The tech giant OpenAI will share its AI cyber defence system Daybreak for free with the Ukraine government to help it protect civilian infrastructure, like hospitals and power plants, from cyber-attacks. According to the Computer Emergency Response Team of Ukraine (CERT-UA), the national cyber incident response team, Ukraine recorded nearly 6,000 attacks in 2025. Daybreak is able to quickly identify weaknesses in digital systems and help develop fixes. Under the deal, Ukraine will get access to OpenAI's advanced GPT 5.6 Sol model - a rival to Anthropic's Mythos and Fable. George Osborne, former UK chancellor and now Head of OpenAI for Countries, said: "Protecting civilian infrastructure means defending it against both physical and digital attacks, so people can continue to live, work and access essential services." Reacting to the news, Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence for the cybersecurity firm Sophos, said that Russian offensive cyber operations had been "a key component" of the Kremlin's aggression against Ukraine since 2014. "Any initiative that strengthens Ukraine's already highly capable, but heavily burdened, cyber defence efforts is a welcome development and could provide a valuable force multiplier," he said. Jamie MacColl, a senior research fellow specialising in cyber at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told the BBC western tech firms had been supporting Ukraine for some time - partly for altruistic reasons but also because they gain very valuable data and intelligence from an active conflict. "Given this, it's no surprise that OpenAI is now also providing defensive cyber security services" he said. He thought access to Daybreak would be useful, particularly given the volume of Russian cyber-attacks targeting the country. But he noted Ukraine already had access to AI tools provided by OpenAI's competitors, like Google. Attack and defence at the frontier The cyber-abilities of the latest, most powerful AI models, called "frontier" models in AI jargon, can be a boon for cyber-defenders, but the same abilities can also be used for attack. Spotting weaknesses in systems, for example, is useful for defenders looking to block hackers, but also for attackers hunting for ways to infiltrate an organisation. Anthropic has tightly restricted access to its systems on the grounds that they are too powerful to fall into the wrong hands, but OpenAI has allowed some firms in Europe, as well as UK banks, to use its most advanced cyber models. The firm made the announcement alongside the UN General Assembly which is currently underway in New York. AI is firmly on the agenda there, and US tech bosses including OpenAI's Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei are due to speak at the high-level gathering. United Nations Secretary General António Guterres called for the tech to be regulated in his final address, while US President Donald Trump says it should be renamed "super intelligence". Evidence suggests the technology is increasingly being used in the Russia-Ukraine conflict. In a report published earlier this month, Anthropic claimed that its Claude platform appeared to have been used by a group of Russian developers to build software for a swarm of so-called "kamikaze" drones designed for attacks in Ukraine. It said the group had activated virtual private networks - VPNs - in order to get around a geographical block put in place by the tech firm. Anthropic also claimed AI had been used in attempts to infiltrate the Ukrainian government, military and diplomatic services. Recently, around 100 US companies signed an open letter warning governments and institutions around the world that "the window is closing" to ensure cyber defences are robust enough to withstand AI-enabled cyber attacks. But it's not just bad actors deploying the tech that are of growing concern: in the summer, OpenAI revealed that a group of AI agents it had been testing had escaped from their controls, and secretly worked together to hack to another tech firm, Hugging Face. Anthropic, and Google subsequently revealed similar incidents. Additional reporting by Chris Vallance Sign up for our Tech Decoded newsletter to follow the world's top tech stories and trends. item.description:

========================================
Angry Anderson, rock star who soundtracked Kylie's wedding in Neighbours, dies aged 79 - Published Rock star Angry Anderson, whose music famously soundtracked the wedding of Kylie Minogue and Jason Donovan's characters in Australian TV soap Neighbours, has died at the age of 79. The musician, whose real name was Gary Anderson, rose to fame as the frontman of Rose Tattoo, one of Australia's most revered rock bands, from 1976. His solo song Suddenly became a global hit after it was played during the wedding of Minogue and Donovan's characters Scott and Charlene in Neighbours. The episode was watched by 20 million people in the UK in 1988. Anderson said Minogue had been "adamant" that the track was used for the scene, and he later declared that Suddenly was the best song he had ever written. Paying tribute to Anderson on Instagram, Donovan said: "Legend! What a great guy. "Another great Australian. Thank you Angry for all the wonderful music and memories. Condolences to all friends and family." Before his death, Anderson had a cardiac arrest while on Rose Tattoo's farewell tour in Europe last month. He was treated in hospital before going home to Australia, and the band cancelled nine live dates. A joint statement, external from Anderson's family and Rose Tattoo remembered him as a "devoted father, and much-loved bandmate". "His loss will be deeply felt by all those who knew and loved him both here in Australia and overseas," it said. "We thank everyone for their prayers and messages of love and continued support." Born in Melbourne in 1947, Anderson and Rose Tattoo first became known on Australia's rock scene, releasing five albums beginning with their 1978 debut. After the band split nine years later, Anderson continued recording music as a solo artist, and co-wrote and released Suddenly in the summer of 1987. It was quickly selected by Minogue for use in Neighbours for her character Charlene Mitchell's wedding to Donovan's Scott Robinson. Thanks in large part to its use in Neighbours, Suddenly reached the top three in both the UK and Australia. However, it was held off the number one spot in its home country by Minogue's own debut solo single, Locomotion. Anderson released two albums as a solo artist, before Rose Tattoo reunited in 1993 to support Guns N' Roses on their Australian tour. The band returned in 1998 for their own tour and were inducted into the Australian Recording Industry Association (ARIA) Hall of Fame in 2006. Anderson's other credits included playing Herod in an Australian production of Jesus Christ Superstar. He was made a Member of the Order of Australia in 1993, in recognition of service to the community, particularly his charity work and his work as a youth advocate. item.title: US to build two military bases in Greenland under new deal with Denmark
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9dr74g32g8go?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US to build two military bases in Greenland under new deal with Denmark - Published The US, Denmark and Greenland have signed a defence deal that allows Washington to build two new military bases in the Arctic territory, while reaffirming Copenhagen's sovereignty over it. Before a signing ceremony at the UN General Assembly in New York, US President Donald Trump said "we will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations". Danish PM Mette Frederiksen said the deal was "good for the US, Denmark and Greenland" and also for Europe and Nato, while Greenland's PM Jens-Frederik Nielsen said it was a "win-win-win". The three leaders then inked the deal, seemingly ending more than a year of tension over the Arctic territory. Trump had threatened to "take" the semi-autonomous Arctic territory over what he said were national security concerns, citing its strategic defence location and its mineral wealth. His rhetoric prompted outcry from Greenlanders, Danes and European leaders who issued a joint statement saying his words "undermine transatlantic relations and risk a dangerous downward spiral". The deal amends and updates a 1951 defence agreement between Denmark and the US. The new pact says the US "shall be allowed to establish an additional Defence Area at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig" - referring to locations in Greenland's south and east. Narsarsuaq is a former civilian airport and World War Two base. It has deep-water access and a large runway which US military engineers were recently surveying, the US North Command confirmed to the BBC. The Mestersvig outpost is remote, far less developed, and used by a Danish naval dog sled unit. The "modalities and technical details" of the bases are yet to be confirmed, and according to the deal, must be mutually agreed by all parties, This means the US security arrangements are not unfettered and Greenland and Denmark's approval is still needed. Washington currently operates its Pituffik Space Base in Greenland's north-west, and the new deal allows the US to "modernise and expand its activities" there. It also says that "no state that is not a member of Nato shall be allowed to establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland nor shall they be allowed a persistent presence of military forces in Greenland". Although the militaries of non-Nato countries are now explicitly barred from the island, it was highly unlikely that non-allied troops would have been allowed access in the first place. Critically, no territory is ceded to the US, and it recognises both Denmark's "sovereignty and territorial integrity" and Greenland's right to self-determination. On one hand, that's a significant climb down from Trump's earlier calls to acquire the Arctic island. But it does deliver a strengthened US military presence and expand on the previous agreement. Therefore to some American eyes, that will be perceived as a historic win. The new deal must still be approved by both Denmark's and Greenland's parliaments. Despite months of crisis, the mood at Tuesday's signing ceremony appeared strikingly upbeat and friendly. "We going to have a tremendous relationship, a secure relationship," Trump said. "This is tremendous for Europe and for the United States, for everybody, and for Greenland it's going to be incredible." Meanwhile, Frederiksen described the signing of the deal as a "milestone in our long-standing co-operation". "Seventy-five years ago we entered into an agreement about the defence of Greenland. Today, we're signing an even bigger and better agreement - a deal that can last forever." The Danish prime minister stressed that the agreement "respects sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenland's right to self-determination". Jens-Frederik Nielsen said that "for Greenland, it is not only an agreement about us, it is [an] agreement with us. "It takes into account the people of Greenland, our rights, our livelihoods and the development of our country. "Greenland matters for North American security and for transatlantic security," he said, adding that the Nato had a key role to play in the North Atlantic in a changing security situation. The agreement also confirmed Greenland would remain in Nato if it were to gain independence from Denmark. The 1951 agreement already allowed the US to send as many troops as it wanted to Greenland. Washington already has more than 100 military personnel permanently stationed at its Pituffik base. Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex Greenland, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China. He argued the Arctic island was an essential piece of his plan to build a futuristic "Golden Dome" defence system to protect the US against missile attacks. However the deal only mentions the project once, and contains no concrete proposal. A Nato spokesperson said shortly afterwards that the military alliance welcomed the deal, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region". In Denmark, the deal is being hailed as a triumph of diplomacy, and several political parties in Denmark have already said they would back it. For Greenland, a country of 56,000 people, there was good reason for a big sigh of relief. Its leader sat side-by-side with the world's most powerful man, and got a deal that should now bring an end to months of crisis. item.description:

========================================
Ukraine anger as EU removes Russian oligarchs from sanctions list - Published The European Union is to remove sanctions on two oligarchs imposed after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to reports, prompting anger in Ukraine. France had campaigned for Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov to be taken off the list, citing "national security concerns". Luxembourg called for the removal of Russian-Israeli businessman Mikhail Fridman, who is suing the country for the release of frozen assets. Latvia initially opposed the deal but agreed to a compromise, part of which involved extending sanctions on nearly 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years. Ukrainian officials said the move was "unacceptable" and sent the wrong signal to Moscow. "Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said on X. He urged all EU member states to instead announce national sanctions on the two individuals. Latvia has already said it would do so. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov earlier welcomed the prospect of the two oligarchs being taken off the list, claiming the EU's sanctions were illegal and all Russians should be removed. Usmanov founded USM Holding company, an investment group that owns iron, steel and copper suppliers, and the Megafon telecommunications company. He has in the past had ties with the English Premier League clubs Arsenal and Everton. The EU froze his assets in 2022, describing him as "a pro-Kremlin oligarch with particularly close ties to Russian president Vladimir Putin". Usmanov said the decision was "unfair". It has been reported that France's initiative was linked to a prospective prisoner release deal with Azerbaijan. Fridman, a Russian-Israeli citizen born in Ukraine, is the founder of the Alfa Group investment conglomerate, with key interests in energy and banking. The EU has described him as a top Russian financier and enabler of Putin's inner circle. Fridman himself said at the time of Russia's full-scale invasion that the conflict should end as soon as possible, but avoided outright condemnation of President Putin. His Russian-Latvian business partner Pyotr Aven was stripped of Latvia's highest civilian honour in 2022 for failing to condemn the invasion of Ukraine. This may have influenced Latvia's opposition to the move, vetoing it in a vote by EU ambassadors on Monday. However, on Tuesday it changed its vote to an abstention as a compromise was reached. The new deal involved extending sanctions on some remaining 2,600 individuals and entities to three years. Until now, sanctions had to be renewed every six months. Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs also announced that France had agreed to start talks with Latvia about joining a French nuclear deterrence initiative and strengthen its military presence in Latvia. - Published15 March 2022 - Published7 March 2022 - Published6 April 2022

item.title: How Ceuta, football and Israel are shaping Morocco's election
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8r4v7n6py97o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
How Ceuta, football and Israel are shaping Morocco's election - Published Disillusioned young voters in Morocco were courted with viral football slogans, promises of one million jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls ahead of Wednesday's parliamentary elections. Yet, for many young Moroccans, politics remains deeply disconnected from reality. "I have no hope for this election. I'm ashamed of our political scene. It's a complete circus," Siham Azeroual, 32, an environmental activist who lives in the Atlas region, tells the BBC. The outcome of the vote will decide the make-up of the next government, just weeks after 60,000 people risked their lives to cross from the North African country to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - a sign of the lack of opportunities many young people feel they have at home. Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy where political parties compete for 395 seats in the House of Representatives, the legislative chamber. Yet executive power remains closely tied to the crown. King Mohammed VI, the 63-year-old monarch, appoints the prime minister from the political party that comes first in the election, but also presides over the Council of Ministers - the country's most important policy-making body. The current campaign also follows a wave of Gen Z protests that erupted in September 2025 over unemployment, healthcare and living costs. Demonstrators chanted slogans like "freedom, dignity, and social justice" which escalated to "get out Akhannouch", a reference to current Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch. More than 2,400 people faced prosecution following the unrest. Despite the crackdown, some young activists are choosing to enter the political arena. Hamza El Kharroubi, 29, was briefly arrested during the protests. He is now running for parliament with the little-known Environment and Sustainable Development Party, which has a green agenda. "As a young person, I don't have much hope. I joined this party because they wanted more Gen Z faces and they are allowing us to speak freely about our demands," El Kharroubi tells the BBC. He comes from Tetouan, just 34km (21 miles) from Fnideq beach, where the migration wave to Ceuta started in late July. Some 60,000 people crossed, both Moroccans and other nationalities. At least 100 people died in the largest migration surge to the enclave in recent history. "We want justice for the families of those who died crossing to Ceuta. We want compensation for their families," El Kharroubi says. He argues that the crossing was widely linked to economic hardship and unemployment. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates overall unemployment stood at 13% last year, while youth unemployment - between the ages of 15 and 24 - reached 37.3%. El Kharroubi says his goal is not to compete with established heavyweights - but securing a voice in parliament to build toward 2031. "As young people, we have to enter the parliament so by 2031 we have strong young politicians who can compete for a seat in the government." Fouzi Lekjaa, head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation and a senior politician who works in the finance ministry, has emerged as the kingdom's newest political sensation - and a definite heavyweight. Credited with helping the Atlas Lions - as the national men's football team is known - become global contenders, Lekjaa joined the centrist Party of Authenticity and Modernity (Pam) in July. Videos of his campaign rallies have gone viral in the football-mad nation that is jointly hosting the next World Cup along with Spain and Portugal. The clips show crowds chanting "Sir" which means "Go" in Moroccan Arabic - the iconic catchphrase from Morocco's historic 2022 World Cup run, when it became the first Arab and African side to make it to the semi-finals. Lekjaa has promised to make Morocco sixth in the world in education and healthcare, to match the Fifa ranking of the men's football team. Pam is competing against 26 other parties, including Prime Minister Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents (RNI). In its bid for a second term, RNI has renewed a pledge to create one million job opportunities by 2031. Political expert Rachid Aourraz, from the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis (MIPA), remains sceptical about this promise. "The slogan 'one million jobs' has become an overused electoral slogan. There is also talk of raising the minimum wage, but what is proposed cannot withstand a structural inability to create stable net jobs," Aourraz tells the BBC. He adds that major parties "do not compete over an alternative model", but rather over how to implement public policies set by a royal vision. Also seeking a political comeback is the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) - using anti-Israeli sentiments to woo voters. Morocco normalised ties with Israel in December 2020 along with several other Arab countries, under the US-brokered Abraham Accords. Led by populist former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane, the PJD is campaigning heavily on a promise to end diplomatic ties with Israel. He says the normalisation was a "mistake" made by his party which led the government between 2016 and 2021. Bilateral ties were hit during the Gaza war with weekly protests taking place in the capital, Rabat, against the Israeli diplomatic presence. During the conflict the Israeli liaison office was closed and direct flights between the two countries were suspended. Yet despite an outpouring of pro-Palestinian protests, with tens of thousands taking to the streets and setting ablaze the Israeli flag at the height of the war, it was announced earlier this month that Israel and Morocco had agreed to open full embassies in their respective countries. This followed a meeting between their top diplomats and the US ambassador to the United Nations. "We have to speak up," Benkirane told supporters at a campaign rally in Marrakesh. "If we work hard, the king will close the Israeli embassy. The king does not like going against his own people," he added, warning of "the dangers of Israel and Zionism in Morocco". I think young people should focus on the microscale: rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top" More than half of Morocco's total population of roughly 38.8 million is under the age of 35 - though only 4% of the more than 15.8 million registered voters are aged between 18 and 24. "I am not keeping up much with the campaigns - but I noticed the same faces as usual," says Hiba, a 27-year-old Moroccan living in Canada who preferred not to use her last name. She lives in Montreal which has a large Moroccan diaspora of about 104,000 people, according to the 2016 census. Many of last year's Gen Z protests were more vocal outside the country, where young Moroccans were able to express their anger without fear of repercussions. Hiba, who co-organised several Gen Z protests in Montreal, says she would have considered voting had she been able to find a proxy in Morocco - which is how those in the diaspora can cast their ballot. "Gen Z protests didn't go in vain. We achieved something. At least now we see more debates with young people on state TV," she says. Azeroual, the environmental activist, agrees. But having lived through both the 20 February movement in 2011 that changed the constitution and the recent Gen Z movement, she believes change must come from a multi-faceted approach. "I think young people should focus on the microscale - rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top," she says. Despite not being fully convinced by any political campaign, she says she will be heading to her local polling station to cast her ballot.
